item.title: 2018: Dodgers beat Brewers 5-1 in Game 7, advance to World Series
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers advanced to the World Series after defeating the Milwaukee Brewers 5–1 in Game 7 of the NLCS at Miller Park. Christian Yelich hit a home run off Dodgers starter Walker Buehler in the first inning to give the Brewers an early lead. Photo: hueytaxi on Flickr (Original version) UCinternational (Crop) (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2020: Umpire Derryl Cousins dies at 74
item.description: Derryl Cousins, 74, Major League Baseball umpire whose career spanned 34 seasons. Photo: ttarasiuk Delaywaves (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2018: Yount threw out the first pitch before Game 7 of the National League
item.description: On October 20, 2018, Yount threw out the first pitch before Game 7 of the National League Championship Series between the Dodgers and Brewers. Photo: Scott Ableman Quakerwildcat at en.wikipedia (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2014: Greg Van Horn named first Field Manager in Jackrabbits history
item.description: On October 20, 2014, Greg Van Horn was named the first Field Manager in Jackrabbits history.

item.title: 2012: Dave May, 68, All-Star outfielder with 12 major league seasons, dies
item.description: Dave May, 68, All-Star outfielder who spent 12 seasons in the majors with the Baltimore Orioles, Milwaukee Brewers, Atlanta Braves, Texas Rangers and Pittsburgh Pirates from 1967 to 1978, and also the player that was sent by Milwaukee to Atlanta in exchange for Hank Aaron. Photo: Baltimore Orioles / MLB (Public domain).

item.title: 2004: Red Sox beat Yankees four straight after losing first three in ALCS
item.description: At Yankee Stadium, the Boston Red Sox pull off one of the greatest comebacks ever, beating the New York Yankees four consecutive times after losing the first three games of the ALCS. Photo: Severin St. Martin (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2004: Chuck Hiller, 70, first NL player to hit World Series grand slam, dies
item.description: Chuck Hiller, 70, second baseman for four NL teams who was that league's first player to hit a grand slam in the World Series (1962, as a San Francisco Giant); longtime coach. Photo: San Francisco Giants / MLB (Public domain).

item.title: 2003: Team renamed Swing of the Quad Cities after another contest
item.description: On October 20, 2003, the team was renamed the "Swing of the Quad Cities"; after another "name the team" contest was held.

item.title: 1999: Calvin Griffith dies at 87, moved Senators to Minnesota
item.description: Calvin Griffith, 87, succeeded uncle Clark Griffith as majority owner, president and de facto general manager of the Washington Senators and their successor, the Minnesota Twins, serving from October 27, 1955, to August 15, 1984; responsible for moving the Senators to Minnesota after the 1960 season. Photo: National Photo Company Collection (Public domain).

item.title: 1990: Reds beat Oakland 2-1, complete stunning World Series sweep
item.description: The talk of an Oakland Athletics dynasty is proven premature, as the Cincinnati Reds beat Oakland 2–1 to complete one of the most stunning sweeps in World Series history. Series MVP José Rijo (2–0, 0.59 ERA) retires 20 batters in a row, Randy Myers getting the last two outs to give the Reds their first World Championship since 1976.

item.title: 1988: Hershiser pitches Dodgers to 5-2 win, World Series title
item.description: Orel Hershiser caps his dream season with a 5–2, four-hitter over the Oakland Athletics in Game 5 of the World Series to give the Dodgers their first championship since 1981 and sixth overall; it also makes them the only team with more than one Fall Classic championship during the 1980s. Hershiser is elected the series' MVP.

item.title: 1988: Dodgers shock Athletics in five games in 1988 World Series
item.description: The playoffs began on October 4, 1988, and concluded on October 20, 1988, with the Dodgers shocking the Athletics in five games in the 1988 World Series.

item.title: 1984: Reds hire Bill Bergesch, 63, as general manager
item.description: The Cincinnati Reds hire longtime executive Bill Bergesch as general manager. Bergesch, 63, had been a member of George Steinbrenner's New York Yankees front office since 1977, and served a brief term (1982–1983) as the Bombers' GM.

item.title: 1981: George Bamberger, 58, named manager of New York Mets
item.description: Pitching guru and former Milwaukee Brewers pilot George Bamberger becomes manager of the New York Mets. Bamberger, 58, led the Brewers to a 235–180 (.566) record between 1978 and 1980. He also served as pitching coach of the Baltimore Orioles for eight seasons when Mets' front-office boss Frank Cashen was Baltimore's top executive. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1979: Cy Slapnicka dies at 93, celebrated Cleveland Indians scout
item.description: Cy Slapnicka, 93, pitcher, scout and executive who spent 60 years in baseball; appeared in only ten total MLB games for 1911 Chicago Cubs and 1918 Pittsburgh Pirates, but became one of the most celebrated scouts of his day working for the Cleveland Indians; signed Hall of Famers Lou Boudreau, fellow Iowan Bob Feller and Bob Lemon among many other stars; general manager of the Indians from 1935 to 1940.

item.title: 1976: Giants and Cardinals make three-for-three trade to open offseason
item.description: The San Francisco Giants and St. Louis Cardinals make a three-for-three trade to kick off the offseason. The Giants send pitchers Mike Caldwell and John D'Acquisto and catcher Dave Rader to the Redbirds for pitcher John Curtis, utilityman Vic Harris and outfielder Willie Crawford. Photo: Milwaukee Brewers (Public domain).

item.title: 1975: Willie Davis traded from Cardinals to Padres for Dick Sharon
item.description: Willie Davis is on the move again. The veteran center fielder is traded from the St. Louis Cardinals to the San Diego Padres for outfielder Dick Sharon. It is Davis' fourth change of address in less than two years. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1972: Allen Russell dies at 72, led American League with nine saves
item.description: Allen Russell, 72, pitcher in 345 games for the New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox and Washington Senators between 1915 and 1925 who led American League with nine saves in 1923; member of 1924 world champion Senators. Photo: National Photo Company Collection (Public domain).

item.title: 1971: California Angels fire general manager Dick Walsh after bad 1971
item.description: The fallout from the California Angels' disastrous 1971 season continues when the club fires general manager Dick Walsh, who has four years remaining on a seven-year contract. Photo: National Photo Company Collection (Public domain).

item.title: 1970: Brewers trade three players to Cardinals for Jim Ellis and Carl Taylor
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers trade pitchers George Lauzerique and Jessie Huggins and catcher Jerry McNertney to the St. Louis Cardinals for left-hander Jim Ellis and catcher Carl Taylor.

item.title: 1965: Mets acquire All-Star third baseman Ken Boyer from Cardinals
item.description: The Mets obtain eleven-time All-Star, 5× Gold Glove-winning third baseman, and 1964 NL Most Valuable Player Ken Boyer, 34, from the St. Louis Cardinals for pitcher Al Jackson and third baseman Charley Smith. Photo: Eric Kilby on Flickr (Original version) SecretName101 (Crop) (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 1933: Lou Gertenrich dies at 58, former Brewers and Pirates outfielder
item.description: Lou Gertenrich, 58. outfielder who played with the Milwaukee Brewers and the Pittsburgh Pirates in a span of two seasons from 1901 to 1903.

item.title: 1923: Syracuse beats Pittsburgh 3-0 in first Yankee Stadium football game
item.description: The first college football game played in Yankee Stadium was a 3-0 Syracuse victory over Pittsburgh on October 20, 1923. Photo: Severin St. Martin (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1906: Buck Ewing dies at 47, Giants catcher and later Cincinnati manager
item.description: Buck Ewing, 47, catcher, most notably for the New York Giants, who batted .303 lifetime and led NL in home runs and triples once each; captain of 1888–1889 NL champions batted .346 in 1888. championship series; in 1883 was one of the first two players to hit 10 home runs in a season; led NL in assists three times and double plays twice, was later Cincinnati manager. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1898: Curry Foley dies at 42, first major leaguer to hit for the cycle
item.description: Curry Foley, 42, Irish outfielder/first baseman/pitcher who played from 1879 through 1883 for the Boston Red Caps and Buffalo Bisons National League teams, and the first major league player ever to hit for the cycle (May 25, 1882). Photo: Howland -- Photographer (Public domain).

item.title: 1888: Giants score five in eighth to beat 6-4 and take 4-1 series lead
item.description: The Giants score five runs in the bottom of the eighth inning to take a 6–4 victory and a 4–1 lead in the series. (World Series results are also recorded for 1886.) Photo: The Library of Congress (No restrictions).

item.title: 1877: Tommy Bond shows curveball curves by throwing around stakes
item.description: Tommy Bond demonstrates proof that a curveball really does curve by throwing it around stakes driven into the ground before an exhibition game. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

item.title: 1874: Boston wins third straight pennant with 14-7 win over Athletic
item.description: The Boston Base Ball Club win their 3rd consecutive pennant with a 14–7 victory over Athletic of Philadelphia. Photo: Tichnor Bros. Inc., Boston, Mass. (Public domain).

item.title: 1864: Jocko Fields born October 20, 1864, American professional player
item.description: John Joseph "Jocko" Fields (October 20, 1864 – October 14, 1950) was an American professional baseball player. Photo: Old Judge (Public domain).
